analysis.one_liner: Strips the EPA's power to regulate greenhouse gas emissions and blocks climate lawsuits.
analysis.headline: A bill to erase the EPA's authority over greenhouse gases won 22 Republican cosponsors, but never got a vote or a hearing in the Senate committee.
analysis.plain_summary: Sen. John Barrasso introduced this bill on January 31, 2011. It would have prohibited the President and every federal agency from issuing or enforcing any regulation of greenhouse gas emissions, and from weighing climate effects in any approval decision, unless the President personally determined the action was needed to protect public health from imminent, direct harm [S2]. It would have nullified the EPA's existing rules limiting greenhouse gases from vehicles, power plants, and other sources [S2], and it would have wiped out common-law lawsuits — court cases brought by states, cities, and citizens claiming that greenhouse gas emissions were a public nuisance — without creating any replacement federal climate policy [S3]. The bill went to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced. It never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 with the bill dead [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Coal, oil, and natural gas producers, and utilities that burn those fuels, are the clear beneficiaries. Greenhouse gas rules are the main policy tool that raises their costs or constrains their output — the bill removes that tool at the federal level [S2], wipes out rules the EPA had already adopted [S2], and shuts down nuisance lawsuits against major emitters [S3]. Energy-intensive manufacturers that pay for compliance would also gain. Ordinary people would see no direct gain in the bill's structure; its stated rationale is lower energy prices and preserved jobs in fossil energy [S3], benefits that would flow through if the bill worked as advertised but which are not guaranteed by its terms.

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits the President and the head of any federal agency from promulgating, enforcing, or implementing any regulation controlling greenhouse gas emissions, or conditioning any approval on climate effects, unless the action is determined necessary to protect public health from imminent and substantial direct harm [S2].

It nullifies every EPA rule and action already issued before enactment to regulate greenhouse gases for their effect on atmospheric concentrations — erasing the rules limiting emissions from vehicles and stationary sources that were in effect in 2011 [S2].

It bars any cause of action based on common-law theories — such as public-nuisance suits seeking money damages or injunctions over greenhouse gas emissions — so no court could impose liability on emitters under state or federal common law [S3].

Supporters' stated rationale is that regulating greenhouse gases under existing federal authority would impose substantial costs on the economy, and that Congress should choose climate policy deliberately rather than leave it to regulators and courts [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The costs fall on the public at large: the health and climate consequences of unrestricted greenhouse gas emissions — the very harms the Clean Air Act rules and the nuisance lawsuits were meant to address — would continue unaddressed, since the bill strips regulators and courts of authority without putting any federal climate policy in its place until Congress separately enacted one [S2] [S3]. People living near power plants and other major emitters would bear the local pollution effects, and future generations bear the climate effects.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, through unaddressed pollution and climate harm

drawbacks.text: The bill removes all federal regulatory and judicial tools over greenhouse gases — Clean Air Act rules and common-law lawsuits alike — while providing no replacement policy, leaving the country with no federal mechanism to address climate change until Congress separately passes one [S2] [S3].
By nullifying rules the EPA had already promulgated, it undoes limits on emissions from vehicles and power plants that were already in force, allowing emissions to rise under pre-2011 standards [S2].

The bill's supporters would argue the cost is real: EPA rules on greenhouse gases raise energy prices and compliance costs for utilities and manufacturers, and supporters contended the agency was exceeding the authority Congress gave it under the Clean Air Act [S3]. An honest supporter would concede that the bill also forecloses the only climate tools available at the time — regulation and litigation — with no guarantee Congress would ever act.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill concentrates its benefits on one sector — fossil-fuel producers and heavy emitters — by removing the regulatory and legal tools that constrain them, while distributing its costs broadly across the public in the form of continued emissions, local air pollution near major sources, and unmitigated climate risk. Because it strips away both regulation and litigation without substituting any policy of its own, the public gives up the only federal climate tools that existed in 2011 and receives nothing specific in return beyond the hope of lower energy prices [S2] [S3].

outcome.mechanism: Introduced January 31, 2011, referred the same day to the Environment and Public Works Committee, and never given a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

narrative.text: Sen. John Barrasso (R-WY) introduced the bill on January 31, 2011, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day [S5].
Twenty-two senators, all Republicans, signed on as cosponsors [S4].
The bill never moved beyond referral: no hearing, no committee report, no floor vote in the two years before the 112th Congress ended [S5].
As a result, the EPA's authority to regulate greenhouse gases under the Clean Air Act and the common-law nuisance cases against major emitters were never affected by this bill [S2] [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The EPA's greenhouse gas rules and the courts' authority over climate-nuisance suits remained untouched, because the bill died in committee. The public kept the regulatory status quo; the fossil-fuel industry and its cosponsors did not get the exemption they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Clean-air rules survived; fossil industry got nothing

for.name: Sen. John Barrasso
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 31, 2011 to strip federal greenhouse gas regulatory authority and preempt climate lawsuits.

for.name: 22 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors of the bill.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and never scheduled a hearing or committee vote on it.

against.name: Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 22 cosponsors were Republicans and the sponsor was a Republican; no Democrat cosponsored, and the Democratic-controlled committee never acted on the bill.

industries.note: Coal-fired power is the most carbon-intensive electricity source, so stripping EPA greenhouse gas authority and nullifying existing rules [S2] relieves coal plants of the emissions limits that constrain them, at the public's expense in pollution and climate harm.

The bill removes the Clean Air Act authority used to limit emissions from vehicles, refineries, and drilling operations, and bars common-law nuisance suits against major emitters [S2] [S3], relieving the sector of both regulatory and litigation costs.

Existing power plants are among the largest regulated emitters; the bill nullifies the rules applying to them and prevents new ones, transferring compliance costs away from the industry to the public [S2].

Greenhouse gas rules create demand for low-carbon electricity; eliminating federal carbon regulation removes that policy advantage relative to fossil generation, though renewables keep any market share won on cost.
